Do not use the action as the start event's label.

When the description's opening sentence states an action that a participant performs to start the process (for example, recognising or identifying a situation), and the process then continues with further described work: Model the stated opening action as a task placed after the start event, so that the start event represents the trigger and the task represents the performed work. Do not use the start event label alone to stand for that action, and do not drop the action from the model.

When the description says that a process ends at its described outcome and that a later occurrence from outside the process, such as feedback or a return, may lead to follow-up work: Do not add a second start event with no incoming sequence flow to the same process to begin a separate start-to-end chain. Model the follow-up work as a message start event in its own process, as an event subprocess, or as a path joined to the main flow through a gateway. The main process keeps only the start event that begins its described flow.

When the description states that, after a party gives approval or acceptance, the process continues to a named follow-on step, and a later recording or confirmation step depends on that follow-on step: Model the named follow-on step as its own task, placed in the sequence between the approval (an intermediate catch event if it is awaited) and the recording or confirmation step. Do not merge the follow-on step into the approval or into the recording step, and preserve the sequence flows that the description implies.
